section.title: The Valley of Dry Bones and One Nation
section.sectionRationale: The book's most iconic vision, dry bones brought to life by the Spirit's breath, answers Israel's despair, 'our hope has perished,' with the promise of national resurrection. The chapter then joins two sticks into one, picturing a reunited people under one King, David's Son, and an everlasting covenant of peace with God's own sanctuary set among them forever.
section.thesis: What looks like a valley of hopelessly dry bones becomes, at the LORD's word and by His Spirit's breath, a vast living army, and what looks like two divided, exiled nations become one people under one Shepherd-King forever, previewing the resurrection life and the reunited, indwelt people of God secured in Jesus Christ.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the valley of dry bones brought to life by prophesied breath; the vision's interpretation as the whole house of Israel's opened graves and God's Spirit given; two sticks joined into one, picturing the reunited nation under one King; and the everlasting covenant of peace, with God's own sanctuary set among His people forever.

units.label: The valley of dry bones
units.note: vision, prophecy to the bones, and prophecy to the breath

verses.text: The hand of the LORD was upon me, and He brought me out by His {{ruach|Spirit}} and set me down in the middle of the valley, and it was full of bones.
He led me all around among them, and I saw a great many bones on the floor of the valley, and indeed, they were very dry.

Then He asked me, “Son of man, can these bones come to life?” 
“O Lord GOD,” I replied, “only You know.”
And He said to me, “Prophesy concerning these bones and tell them, ‘{{atsamot_yeveshot|Dry bones}}, hear the word of the LORD!
This is what the Lord GOD says to these bones: I will cause breath to enter you, and you will come to life.
I will attach tendons to you and make flesh grow upon you and cover you with skin. I will put breath within you so that you will come to life. Then you will know that I am the LORD.’”
So I prophesied as I had been commanded. And as I prophesied, there was suddenly a noise, a rattling, and the bones came together, bone to bone.
As I looked on, tendons appeared on them, flesh grew, and skin covered them; but there was no breath in them.

Then He said to me, “Prophesy to the breath; prophesy, son of man, and tell the breath that this is what the Lord GOD says: Come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe into these slain, so that they may live!”
So I prophesied as He had commanded me, and the breath entered them, and they came to life and stood on their feet, a vast army.

units.label: My people, I will open your graves
units.note: the vision interpreted: national resurrection and My Spirit given

verses.text: Then He said to me, “Son of man, these bones are the whole house of Israel. Look, they are saying, ‘Our bones are dried up, and our hope has perished; we are cut off.’
Therefore prophesy and tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘O My people, I will open your graves and bring you up from them, and I will bring you back to the land of Israel.
Then you, My people, will know that I am the LORD, when I open your graves and bring you up from them.
I will put My {{ruach|Spirit}} in you and you will live, and I will settle you in your own land. Then you will know that I, the LORD, have spoken, and I will do it, declares the LORD.’”

units.label: The two sticks made one
units.note: one nation, one king, cleansed forever

verses.text: Again the word of the LORD came to me, saying,

“And you, son of man, take a single stick and write on it: ‘Belonging to Judah and to the Israelites associated with him.’ Then take another stick and write on it: ‘Belonging to Joseph, the stick of Ephraim, and to all the house of Israel associated with him.’
Then join them together into one stick, so that they become one in your hand.
When your people ask you, ‘Won't you explain to us what you mean by these?’

you are to tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘I will take the stick of Joseph, which is in the hand of Ephraim, and the tribes of Israel associated with him, and I will put them together with the stick of Judah. I will make them into a single stick, and they will become one in My hand.’
When the sticks on which you write are in your hand and in full view of the people,

you are to tell them that this is what the Lord GOD says: ‘I will take the Israelites out of the nations to which they have gone, and I will gather them from all around and bring them into their own land.

I will make them {{goy_echad|one nation}} in the land, on the mountains of Israel, and one king will rule over all of them. Then they will no longer be two nations and will never again be divided into two kingdoms.

They will no longer defile themselves with their idols or detestable images, or with any of their transgressions. I will save them from all their apostasies by which they sinned, and I will cleanse them. Then they will be My people, and I will be their God.

units.label: One shepherd, an everlasting covenant, My sanctuary among them
units.note: My servant David king forever, God dwelling with His people

verses.text: My servant David will be king over them, and there will be one shepherd for all of them. They will follow My ordinances and keep and observe My statutes.

They will live in the land that I gave to My servant Jacob, where your fathers lived. They will live there forever with their children and grandchildren, and My servant David will be their prince forever.
And I will make a covenant of peace with them; it will be an everlasting covenant. I will establish them and multiply them, and I will set My sanctuary among them forever.
My dwelling place will be with them; I will be their God, and they will be My people.
Then the nations will know that I the LORD sanctify Israel, when My sanctuary is among them forever.’”

ruach.gloss: Breath, wind, and Spirit, one Hebrew word doing all three jobs at once. The vision's power depends on this single word's range: the same ruach that gives physical breath is the ruach God puts within His people as His own Spirit.

atsamot_yeveshot.gloss: Dry bones, the picture of total, hopeless death, chosen deliberately as the least likely candidate for life by any natural means, so that only God's own word and Spirit can explain what happens next.

goy_echad.gloss: One nation, ending the division into two kingdoms (Israel and Judah) that had marked Israel's history since Solomon's death, reunited here under one King forever.

basic.context: Ezekiel is set down in a valley littered with very dry bones, the picture of Israel's own despair: 'our bones are dried up, our hope has perished, we are cut off.' At God's command Ezekiel prophesies first to the bones, then to the breath itself, and a vast army stands to life. God explains: this is the whole house of Israel, and He will open their graves, put His own Spirit in them, and settle them in their land. Then two sticks, Judah and Joseph, are joined into one in Ezekiel's hand, picturing a reunited nation under one King, David's Son, forever.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a vision, not a literal event witnessed by others, given to answer Israel's specific despair over the exile with the promise of national restoration; the chapter itself interprets its own symbolism plainly, 'these bones are the whole house of Israel' (v11) and 'these sticks... will become one in My hand' (v19). Its language of graves opened and breath given also anticipates, without exhausting, the New Testament's teaching on bodily resurrection and the gift of the Spirit.
basic.originalLanguages: The vision turns entirely on one word played three ways: ruach, meaning breath, wind, and Spirit all at once. The same ruach that must enter the atsamot yeveshot, dry bones, to give them life is the ruach God promises to put within His people so they will live, verse 14, the very word Genesis uses for the breath of life breathed into Adam, Genesis 2:7. The two sticks joined become goy echad, one nation, ending forever the division into two kingdoms.
basic.typology: Physical resurrection from dry bones is a direct, deliberate preview of bodily resurrection, most fully realized in Christ's own rising, the firstfruits of everyone who belongs to Him, 1 Corinthians 15:20-23, and in the resurrection of all the dead at His return, John 5:28-29. The reuniting of Judah and Joseph into one nation under one King anticipates Christ breaking down the dividing wall of hostility to create one new humanity in Himself, Ephesians 2:14-16.
basic.christ: Jesus is both the source of the ruach that raises dead bones to life, breathing His Spirit on His disciples after the resurrection, John 20:22, and the pattern and guarantee of resurrection itself: 'I am the resurrection and the life,' John 11:25. He is also 'My servant David', the one King appointed forever over the reunited nation, Ezekiel 37:24-25, the Son of David whose kingdom has no end, Luke 1:32-33.
basic.god: God is the God who speaks life into what is beyond hope, dry, disjointed bones with no natural capacity to live, and He does it by His own word and His own Spirit's breath, not by any latent potential in the bones themselves. He is equally the God who reunites what sin and history had divided, Israel and Judah, into one people under one King, sealed by an everlasting covenant and His own presence dwelling among them forever.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 2:7 records God breathing the breath of life into Adam, the same word and act echoed here. Ephesians 2:14-16 shows Christ making two into one new humanity. John 11:25 has Jesus declaring Himself the resurrection and the life. 1 Corinthians 15:20-23 grounds all future bodily resurrection in Christ's own.
basic.oneStory: This is Scripture's most vivid picture of hope beyond hope: a valley of dry bones, hopeless by every natural measure, stands up as a living army at God's word and Spirit's breath, and a divided, exiled people is reunited under one King forever. It anticipates and guarantees the resurrection life and undivided people of God secured in Jesus Christ, who is Himself the resurrection, the one Shepherd-King, and the dwelling place of God with man.

context.literary:
Chapter 37 is the third movement of a run that began at chapter 33, where a fugitive arrives with the news that the city has been struck down. Chapter 34 promised a shepherd, chapter 36 promised a new heart and a new spirit, and chapter 37 stages those promises as drama. The passage has two panels joined by a shared ending. The first is a vision, verses 1 to 14, in which Ezekiel sees and speaks. The second is a sign act, verses 15 to 28, in which he handles two pieces of wood and explains them. Both panels end in the same place, with God settling a people in their land and living among them.

Within the vision the action is carefully staged in two commands. The first prophecy to the bones produces sound, sinew, flesh and skin, a body with no life in it, verses 7 and 8. Only the second prophecy, addressed to the breath itself, produces a living army, verses 9 and 10. The narrator slows the reader down at exactly the point where a quicker story would have rushed to the happy ending. Then God interprets the picture in verses 11 to 14, and the words of despair the exiles had been saying are turned back on them as the text of a promise.

The sign act is quieter. Ezekiel's earlier symbolic acts were harsh, a siege model, a shaved head, a packed bag. This one only asks him to write a name on each of two sticks and hold them end to end until they cling together. The closing oracle in verses 24 to 28 piles up the great covenant words, one shepherd, my servant David, an everlasting covenant of peace, my sanctuary, forever. The word forever keeps returning through verses 25 to 28, and it is the hinge into the temple vision that follows in chapters 40 to 48.
context.historical:
Ezekiel was a priest deported to Babylon with King Jehoiachin in 597 BC, and he prophesied among exiles by the canal Chebar. For the first years of his ministry he told them Jerusalem would fall, and they did not believe him. Once the news of 586 BC arrived, 33:21, the problem reversed. Now the exiles believed him entirely, and their trouble was that they could see no future. The words in 37:11, our bones are dried up, our hope has perished, we are cut off, are what a defeated people say when the temple is ash, the Davidic throne is empty, and the land belongs to others.

The picture of unburied bones would have struck first hearers hard. In Israel's world, to lie unburied and exposed was the mark of a catastrophe, and Jeremiah had threatened that very fate for Jerusalem's leaders, Jeremiah 8:1 and 2. Ezekiel was himself a priest, and the law made contact with bones a source of seven days of uncleanness, Numbers 19:16. That God leads a priest around and among the bones, 37:2, is a deliberate and unsettling detail.

The two sticks answer an older wound. After Solomon's death the kingdom had split around 930 BC into a northern realm led by Ephraim, the tribe of Joseph's son, and a southern realm led by Judah. The north was carried off by Assyria in 722 BC and its people scattered, and the south was now carried off by Babylon. The promise that these two would again be one in their own land overturned centuries of separation, and it matches what other prophets had said, Isaiah 11:13, Jeremiah 3:18, Hosea 1:11.
context.canonical:
Within Ezekiel the vision is the answer to chapter 36. The promise there of a new heart and God's own Spirit within, 36:26 and 27, is enacted here as breath entering bodies, 37:14, and the cleansing of 36:25 to 28 becomes the covenant keeping of 37:23 and 24. The promise of one shepherd, my servant David, in 34:23 and 24 returns word for word in 37:24, and the covenant of peace of 34:25 becomes an everlasting covenant of peace in 37:26. The sanctuary promised among them forever then becomes the whole subject of chapters 40 to 48, and the river and the city's name, The LORD is there, close the book, 48:35.

Beyond Ezekiel, the image of life out of the dust is picked up by later prophecy. Isaiah 26:19 says your dead will live, their bodies will rise, and Daniel 12:2 says many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake. Hosea had already pictured Israel's revival as a raising up after two days and a third, Hosea 6:2. None of these quotes Ezekiel, but they share the same grammar of hope, and by the time of the New Testament the passage was a natural place to turn when speaking of rising from the dead.

The New Testament uses the chapter in at least three ways. Jesus says the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God and live, John 5:25, which reads like Ezekiel's command to the bones to hear the word of the LORD. Paul quotes 37:27 to tell the Corinthians that the church is the temple of the living God, 2 Corinthians 6:16. And Revelation 11:11 describes breath of life from God entering two slain witnesses so that they stood on their feet, using the same pattern as 37:10.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Ezekiel wanted the exiles to give up a particular sentence, we are cut off, and to take up another, you will know that I am the LORD. The chapter is not a general comfort about life after death. It is a direct reply to a defeated community that had decided God's promises to Abraham, David and Sinai had run out. The first move is to make them look at their own despair honestly. God does not tell the bones they are not dead. He lets Ezekiel walk among them until he has counted how dry they are, and he asks the question the people would not ask, can these bones come to life?

The prophet's answer, only You know, is the right posture. He does not say yes, and he does not say no. He hands the question back to the one who can answer it, and the rest of the chapter shows that the answer lies in the word God speaks and the breath God gives, not in anything the bones possess. The recurring purpose clause, then you will know that I am the LORD, in verses 6, 13 and 14, tells the first hearers what response is wanted: trust in a God who keeps His word by acting.

The second half asks for something concrete as well. A people who had been two kingdoms were to hear that they would be one under one shepherd, and that this unity would come with obedience, they will follow my ordinances, verse 24. Ezekiel meant the exiles to leave the vision with their hope restored and their idols renounced, verse 23.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The vision describes what God promises to do, and the sign act describes what Ezekiel was commanded to do. Neither is a method for anyone else to repeat. No reader is told to preach to a cemetery, and the chapter does not turn into a technique for reviving a church or a nation by prophesying at it. What the passage prescribes for its hearers is a response: hear the word of the LORD, verse 4, give up the idols, verse 23, and expect God to do what He has said, verse 14.

The text also mixes what it says plainly with what it says in picture. God Himself tells us how to read the bones, they are the whole house of Israel, verse 11, and how to read the sticks, verse 19. A careful reader stays within those given keys. The opened graves of verse 12 are a picture of national restoration in its first sense, and the New Testament's teaching on bodily resurrection builds on the same pattern without making Ezekiel say it directly. For the believer now, the application is to bring our own dry places, a dead marriage, a barren church, a hopeless diagnosis, to the God who asks us the same question and to answer as Ezekiel did, only You know, and then to keep speaking the word He has given.

debates.question: Does the vision teach only national restoration, or also bodily resurrection?

views.label: National restoration only
views.case: God interprets the bones for us in verse 11 as the whole house of Israel, and the despair in view is political, we are cut off. The opened graves of verse 12 end with a return to the land of Israel, not with a general rising. On this reading the picture is a metaphor of revival from exile, and resurrection doctrine is imported from elsewhere.

views.label: National restoration that presupposes resurrection
views.case: A metaphor works only if the thing pictured is thinkable. Israel's hearers could be asked to imagine the dead standing on their feet because the idea of God raising the dead was part of what they could picture, and the later texts of Isaiah 26:19 and Daniel 12:2 draw on the same stock of imagery. The primary meaning stays national, but the metaphor carries a real hope with it.

views.label: A vision of the resurrection itself
views.case: Some early Jewish and Christian readers heard the chapter as a straightforward promise of the final resurrection, and the church has long read it at Easter. The language of graves, breath and standing up fits that reading, but verses 11 to 14 are hard to square with it unless the national sense is kept.

debates.bearing: The text's own interpretation settles the first reading, and the New Testament shows that a deeper pattern was always inside it. Holding the national sense as the meaning and the resurrection as the extension honors both the author's words and the way Scripture later uses them.

debates.question: Who is the David of verses 24 and 25?

views.label: A future Davidic king
views.case: David had been dead for centuries, so My servant David must be a descendant who rules as the one shepherd. This is how Jeremiah 23:5 and 6 and Hosea 3:5 speak, and it fits the title nasi, prince, in verse 25, which Ezekiel uses for the ruler throughout the temple chapters.

views.label: The Messiah Himself
views.case: The promise is for a king who rules forever, and no merely human son of David met that description. The New Testament identifies this King as Jesus, the Son of David whose kingdom has no end, Luke 1:32 and 33, and the one shepherd of John 10:16 plainly echoes the one shepherd here.

views.label: David returned in a descendant
views.case: A few have read the name as a literal return of David, as the one who is raised to rule his people. Most interpreters reject this because Ezekiel's own phrase in 34:24 sets David as prince among the people, with the LORD as their God.

debates.bearing: The first two views are not rivals. A future son of David is promised, and the New Testament names Him. The text never says David himself will be raised.

debates.question: When is the two into one fulfilled?

views.label: In the return from exile
views.case: Some Judahites and some northerners went back under Cyrus, and the post exilic community called itself Israel. The sticks were joined, on this reading, in the restored community of Ezra and Nehemiah, though imperfectly.

views.label: In Christ and the church
views.case: The New Testament says Christ made the two groups one, Ephesians 2:14 to 16, and gathered other sheep into one flock, John 10:16. The new covenant and the Spirit of verse 14 are present facts for believers.

views.label: In a future regathering
views.case: Others see a final, national fulfillment because the passage speaks of land, king and temple in terms that were never realized in the second temple period. Verses 25 to 28 say forever, and no previous return lasted.

debates.bearing: Because the promise has a sign in each age, most readers hold more than one of these together. The fullness lies in the one shepherd, and in that sense the church shares in the fulfillment now while the last chapter of the story is still to come.

study.originalLanguages:
Start with the verb that governs the whole chapter, nabe', to prophesy. Ezekiel is told to prophesy to bones, to breath, and then to his people, and the same verb is used for all three. The command is unusual in that its audience cannot hear it. The prophet speaks to a pile of remains, and the narrative reports obedience first and result second, verse 7. That is how the passage makes its point about the power of the spoken word of God.

The second word is the one that keeps the exile's despair on the page, tikvah, hope. The people's complaint, our hope has perished, uses a word that elsewhere means the thing one waits for, as in Jeremiah 29:11, a future and a hope. God does not rebuke the complaint. He accepts that the old hope has died, and He gives a new one with a new ground. The same complaint says we are cut off, and the sense is of being severed from the body of the people, from the covenant line, and from the land. The sticks answer this severing with a joining, so the two halves of the chapter fit as a diagnosis and a cure.

Third, notice the verb in verses 12 and 13, 'alah, to bring up. Israel's founding verb is here, the one God used when He promised to bring His people up out of Egypt, Exodus 3:8. The exile is spoken of as a second Egypt, and the grave becomes the house of slavery from which God draws His people out. The plain meaning of graves as the place of the exile and the resonance with the exodus work together.

Fourth, verse 9 says breathe into these slain, harugim, people killed by violence, not people who died quietly. The army that stands is made of casualties. Together with the vast army of verse 10, chayil, a word for a force of fighting strength, this suggests that what God raises is not just survivors but a people with a strength they had lost.

Last, the covenant words of verses 26 and 27. The phrase is berit shalom, a covenant of peace, the same pair used in 34:25, Numbers 25:12 and Isaiah 54:10, and it is called a berit olam, an everlasting covenant. The promise, My dwelling place will be with them, uses mishkan, the tabernacle word, as in Leviticus 26:11, where the BSB renders it dwelling place. The same chapter that raises bones ends by giving back the tent of God among His people.

typology.type: Dry bones raised by word and breath, Ezekiel 37:1-10
typology.fulfillment: The two stage creation, body first and breath second, mirrors Genesis 2:7, where God forms the man from dust and then breathes into him. Christ is the one who does this at the end. He breathes on His disciples and says receive the Holy Spirit, John 20:22, and He says the dead will hear His voice and live, John 5:25. Paul adds that the Spirit who raised Jesus will give life to mortal bodies, Romans 8:11. The type falls short in that Ezekiel's army lives only to face another death, while those raised in Christ are raised to an imperishable body, 1 Corinthians 15:42 to 44.

typology.type: The opened graves and the coming up to the land, Ezekiel 37:12-14
typology.fulfillment: God promises to open the graves and bring His people up. This pattern comes to a head at the empty tomb, where the stone is rolled away and the first fruits of the dead rise, 1 Corinthians 15:20 to 23. Jesus calls Lazarus out of a grave, John 11:43 and 44, as a sign that He will do this for all who sleep in Him, John 5:28 and 29. The land to which Israel returns becomes, in the New Testament, a new creation in which the people of God live forever. The type falls short because the return from Babylon, which was historical, did not finish the work.

typology.type: Two sticks, Judah and Joseph, joined in one hand, Ezekiel 37:15-22
typology.fulfillment: The two sticks picture one people made of two, held together not by their own effort but in the hand of God, verse 19. Paul describes how Christ made two groups one, tearing down the dividing wall of hostility to create one new man out of the two, Ephesians 2:14 to 16, and Jesus speaks of other sheep that will join one flock under one shepherd, John 10:16. The type is limited, since the sticks join two sections of a single family while the new unity reaches across every people, Revelation 7:9.

typology.type: My servant David as one shepherd and prince forever, Ezekiel 37:24-25
typology.fulfillment: David is the type of the king, and his throne is the form in which God's rule over the people is promised to last. Jesus is the Good Shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep, John 10:11, and the great Shepherd brought back from the dead through the blood of the eternal covenant, Hebrews 13:20. The type falls short in that the historic David died and his sons failed. The fulfillment is a king who rises and does not die, and the shepherd of this chapter is also the sacrifice.

typology.type: My dwelling place will be with them, Ezekiel 37:26-28
typology.fulfillment: The sanctuary set among the people forever is fulfilled when the Word becomes flesh and tabernacles among us, John 1:14, and then in the church, which Paul calls the temple of the living God, citing this very verse, 2 Corinthians 6:16. It reaches its end in the voice from the throne that says the dwelling of God is with man, Revelation 21:3. The type falls short because any physical sanctuary can be destroyed, and the final dwelling is God with His people with no building between them.

study.christ:
The chapter points to Christ at four places, and it helps to take them in the order Ezekiel gives them. The first is the Spirit. Ezekiel is brought out by the Spirit, instructed to speak to the breath, and told that God will put His Spirit in the people, verse 14. John records that on the evening of the resurrection Jesus breathed on His disciples and said receive the Holy Spirit, John 20:22, a gesture that recalls the Lord who breathed into Adam, Genesis 2:7, and who commands the breath in this vision. Paul calls the risen Jesus the last Adam, a life giving spirit, 1 Corinthians 15:45, and says that the Spirit of the One who raised Jesus lives in believers and will give life to their mortal bodies, Romans 8:11. The dry bones passage is in this sense a preview of the gift that Jesus gives after He has risen.

The second is the word. Ezekiel's task is to say hear the word of the LORD to the dead, and the dead stand up. In John 5:25 Jesus says the hour is coming and has now come when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live. At Bethany He stands before a tomb and calls Lazarus by name, John 11:43. The prophet commands bones in the name of the Lord, and Jesus speaks as the Lord, with the authority that raises the dead. This is where the pattern reaches a person who does what the vision only portrays.

The third is the shepherd king. Chapter 37 gathers Ezekiel's promise of one shepherd from chapter 34 and one king from the line of David. Jesus says I am the good shepherd, John 10:11, and speaks of other sheep that will be brought into one flock, John 10:16. Hebrews names Him that great Shepherd of the sheep, brought back from the dead through the blood of the eternal covenant, Hebrews 13:20, and the phrase is a near echo of the everlasting covenant in verse 26. Gabriel promises Mary that her son will receive the throne of His father David and reign forever, Luke 1:32 and 33.

The fourth is the dwelling. The final promise is My dwelling place will be with them, verse 27. John 1:14 says the Word became flesh and tabernacled among us, and Paul quotes this verse of Ezekiel to the Corinthians as true of the church, 2 Corinthians 6:16. We should not turn each bone and sinew into a symbol of something in Christ. The link is in the pattern, a people dead beyond human help are raised by the word and Spirit of God and gathered under one shepherd king who lives among them.
study.god:
The God of this chapter is the God who asks questions He has already answered. He asks Ezekiel can these bones live, and He does not seem to need the answer. The question is a way of bringing the prophet, and through him the exiles, to the place where they must say only You know. A God who asks in this way is not unaware of the facts. He is leading His people to see that the power lies with Him.

He is the God of the word. Everything the chapter shows happens because He speaks and His prophet repeats it. The bones rattle, the sinews appear and the flesh grows as the word is spoken, and the second word brings the breath. It is a picture of creation by speech, Genesis 1, now turned to re creation. This tells us how He works, which is by a word that does what it says, and it tells us that the word is not a mere message but a power.

He is the God who gives His own Spirit and not just a gift from Him. The key line is I will put My Spirit in you and you will live, verse 14. Life is not a resource He dispenses from a distance. It is His own breath, His own presence, given into the people. This anticipates the doctrine of the Holy Spirit as the one who gives life, and it shows why the New Testament can speak of the Spirit and the life together, Romans 8:11.

He is faithful to a covenant that the people had broken. The whole house of Israel is to be gathered and made one, not because they have earned it but because He has sworn it. The covenant of peace is everlasting, and His sanctuary is among them forever, verses 26 to 28. The exile was the judgment of a holy God, and the return is the work of the same God keeping a promise He made before the exile.

He is the God who acts so that He may be known. The phrase you will know that I am the LORD closes the first half of the chapter twice, and in verse 28 the nations will know that He sanctifies Israel. What He does for His people is not private. It is visible to the world, and it is the way He makes Himself known.

For worship, the passage teaches us to bring dry places to this God without softening them. The exiles said their bones were dried up, and God took them at their word. We can pray honestly about what looks dead and then wait on the God who alone knows.

crossReferences.note: God forms the man from the dust and breathes into his nostrils the breath of life. Ezekiel's two stage vision, a body assembled and then breath given, is a deliberate echo of the first creation, now applied to a people who have lost their life.

The promise of a new heart and God's Spirit within, so that His people will walk in His statutes. Chapter 37 stages this promise as a picture, and verse 14 repeats it in nearly the same words, I will put My Spirit in you.

God will appoint one shepherd, My servant David, who will feed His flock. The same figure appears in 37:24 and 25, and the repeated pairing of servant David with the shepherd and the prince ties the two chapters together.

Your dead will live; their bodies will rise. Isaiah and Ezekiel use the same language of dwellers in the dust waking up, and the two together shaped later Jewish and Christian hope for a bodily resurrection.

Many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life. Daniel states in plain words what Ezekiel pictures, that the dead will rise, and Daniel applies it to individuals as well as to the nation.

The people of Judah and of Israel will be gathered together and appoint one leader. Hosea, writing to the northern kingdom before its fall, already promised the reunion that Ezekiel dramatizes with two sticks.

Jesus says the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live. The pattern of speaking to the dead and the dead hearing and living is the very pattern of Ezekiel 37:4 and 5, now said of Christ.

On the evening of the resurrection Jesus breathes on His disciples and says receive the Holy Spirit. The breath that Ezekiel was told to call from the four winds is here given by Christ Himself to His people.
If the Spirit of the One who raised Jesus lives in you, He will also give life to your mortal bodies. Paul states the hope of Ezekiel 37:14 as a present fact with a future result.
Christ is our peace, who made the two one and tore down the dividing wall of hostility. This is the new covenant meaning of the two sticks joined, one new humanity from two, reconciled in one body.

Paul tells the Corinthians that we are the temple of the living God and quotes God's words, I will dwell with them and walk among them. He takes Ezekiel 37:27, with Leviticus 26:12, as a promise now fulfilled in the church.

After three and a half days the breath of life from God entered the two witnesses, and they stood on their feet. John draws deliberately on Ezekiel 37:10, showing that the vision is still the pattern for how God vindicates His people.

study.oneStory:
Scripture's story has a shape that Ezekiel 37 makes unusually clear: life given, life lost, life given again. In Genesis 2:7 God breathes into dust and a man becomes a living being. In Genesis 3 the man is told that he will return to dust. From that point the Bible is the story of whether God will breathe again. The exile is the nation level version of the fall, with a people driven from the land and cut off from the presence, and this chapter is the answer, a vision in which the dust of a people is raised, and the Spirit comes into it.

The chapter also answers two questions that the story has been asking since the early pages. The first is whether the family that began with Abraham can be one. The division after Solomon and the loss of the north made that look impossible, and the promise of one stick answers it. The second is whether the promised king from David's line will ever reign, and Ezekiel's answer is that one shepherd will rule over all of them. Both questions belong to the covenant that began with Abraham, 2 Samuel 7 and Genesis 12, and Ezekiel says they will be fulfilled.

It sets up what comes next. The promise of a sanctuary among them forever leads straight into the temple vision of chapters 40 to 48. The Spirit put within the people leads to the new covenant of Jeremiah 31 and the day of Pentecost. The one shepherd and the one flock lead to John 10 and Ephesians 2. And the raising of the dead leads to the empty tomb and to the resurrection of all who belong to Christ, 1 Corinthians 15:20 to 23.

In the new creation the picture is complete. The breath of life enters a people who had been dead, and they stand on their feet. There is no more division, because people from every tribe and language stand before one throne, Revelation 7:9. There is one shepherd, the Lamb, Revelation 7:17. And God's dwelling is with man, so that He is their God and they are His people, Revelation 21:3, the exact words of Ezekiel 37:27. The valley of the dead is turned into a city of the living, and the story that began with breath ends with breath, as the sign of the God who gives life.

sermon.title: The God Who Makes Alive
sermon.why: Keller preaches directly from Ezekiel 37:1-14, the valley of dry bones, tracing exactly the movement from hopeless death to Spirit-given life this study centers on, and its anticipation of resurrection life secured fully in Christ.

quiz.q: What despairing words does Ezekiel record the exiles saying about themselves, verse 11?

options.text: 'Our bones are dried up, and our hope has perished; we are cut off.'
options.note: Verse 11 records exactly these words as the despair the vision directly answers.

options.text: 'The city has been taken and we are shamed forever.'
options.note: That report belongs to Ezekiel 33:21; this chapter's despair is expressed differently, as hope perished and being cut off.

options.text: 'Our God has abandoned this land completely.'
options.note: The recorded despair concerns the people's own hope and standing, not a claim that God abandoned the land.

options.text: No specific words are recorded; only the vision itself is described.
options.note: The chapter records specific, quoted words of despair directly in verse 11.

quiz.q: In what order does life return to the bones, according to verses 7-10?

options.text: Bones come together, then tendons, flesh, and skin appear, and only afterward does breath enter them to bring them to life.
options.note: Verses 7-10 describe exactly this sequence, physical form first, breath entering last.

options.text: Breath enters first, and the physical body forms around it afterward.
options.note: The sequence is reversed from this; physical form comes first, and breath only afterward brings it to life.

options.text: Everything happens simultaneously in a single instant.
options.note: The text describes a distinct two-stage process, physical assembly and then a separate act of prophesying to the breath.

options.text: The bones are described as never actually receiving physical form, only symbolic hope.
options.note: The bones visibly receive tendons, flesh, and skin, verse 8, before the account of breath entering them.

quiz.q: What does God explicitly promise to do in verse 14, alongside opening the graves?

options.text: Put His Spirit in them so they will live, and settle them in their own land.
options.note: Verse 14 states both promises directly and together.

options.text: Give them a new set of written laws to obey.
options.note: The promise concerns God's own Spirit and resettlement in the land, not a new law code.

options.text: Send a new prophet to replace Ezekiel among them.
options.note: No replacement prophet is mentioned; the promise concerns the Spirit and the land.

options.text: Nothing further is promised beyond opening the graves.
options.note: Verse 14 explicitly adds two further promises, the Spirit given and settlement in the land.

quiz.q: What do the two sticks, for Judah and for Joseph/Ephraim, symbolize once joined together, verses 15-22?

options.text: That God will make His people one nation in the land, no longer divided into two kingdoms.
options.note: Verse 22 states this explicitly as the meaning of the joined sticks.

options.text: That the northern and southern kingdoms will remain permanently separate but allied.
options.note: The text explicitly promises they will 'no longer be two nations,' the opposite of remaining separate.

options.text: That the ten lost tribes would never be found or restored.
options.note: The sign promises the opposite: full reunification of all the tribes into one nation.

options.text: The sticks are purely decorative and carry no symbolic meaning.
options.note: The chapter explicitly interprets the sticks' meaning in verses 19 and 22; they are not merely decorative.

quiz.q: Who is appointed as king over the reunited nation forever, and what covenant does God make with them, verses 24-26?

options.text: God's servant David is king and shepherd forever, under an everlasting covenant of peace with God's sanctuary set among them forever.
options.note: Verses 24-26 state each of these elements directly and together.

options.text: A council of elders governs the nation collaboratively without any king.
options.note: A specific individual king, 'My servant David,' is named directly, not a council.

options.text: Ezekiel himself is appointed as the permanent ruling prophet-king.
options.note: The appointed king is named as 'My servant David,' not Ezekiel.

options.text: No king or covenant is mentioned in this section.
options.note: Both a specific king and a specific everlasting covenant are named explicitly in verses 24-26.

questions: The exiles said, 'our hope has perished; we are cut off,' yet God had resurrection life waiting for them all along. What situation in your life feels like dry bones, beyond any natural hope of recovery?

God's Spirit had to enter the reassembled bodies before they could truly live; flesh and form alone were not enough. Where in your own life have you tried to arrange all the right pieces without depending on God's own Spirit to bring actual life?

Two divided, once-hostile groups, Judah and Joseph, are joined into one people in Ezekiel's own hand at God's command. What division, in your family, church, or community, do you need to trust God to heal rather than resigning yourself to permanent separation?

God promises His own sanctuary, His dwelling, will be among His people forever. How does knowing God's own presence, not just His promises, is what secures your future change how you face an uncertain day?
This vision answers total despair with total, resurrection-level hope. Where do you need to preach this same promise to your own heart this week rather than simply agreeing with it as a nice idea?

translationNotes.note: 'By His Spirit' translates the same Hebrew word, ruach, rendered 'breath' and 'wind' later in the chapter; the single word's range (breath, wind, Spirit) is essential to the vision's meaning and cannot be fully captured by any single English word throughout.

'We are cut off' uses a Hebrew verb often applied to being cut off from the covenant community entirely; the exiles' despair was not merely emotional but a fear of total covenant exclusion, which God's promise directly answers.

The 'stick' in this acted-out sign was likely a flat wooden tablet suitable for writing a name on and holding alongside another, a simple visual aid Ezekiel could join together in one hand before the watching exiles.
